fixes.explanation: That's the one, baker. Melchizedek does the blessing here. The writer says he met Abraham, forefather of Israel, returning from the slaughter of the kings, "…and blessed him…" (Hebrews 7:1). Keep an eye on which way that blessing goes, because the writer leans on it in verse 7.

Close, baker, but the direction is flipped. It's Melchizedek who blesses Abraham, not the other way around. The writer says Melchizedek "…met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him…" (Hebrews 7:1). Easy to flip, like mixing up who hands over the cookie and who gets it.

The plunder does come up, but the writer never says a word about Abraham's riches here. His point is right there in the verse: "Consider how great Melchizedek was…" (Hebrews 7:4). Abraham giving him a tenth is what the writer points to as showing Melchizedek's greatness. Abraham's bank account isn't the star of this verse.

Aaron is a fair name to think of, baker, but the writer names only Melchizedek and Abraham in this meeting (Hebrews 7:1). He says "…the lesser is blessed by the greater." (Hebrews 7:7). Abraham is the one who got blessed, so he's the lesser one there. Aaron's name comes up later, in verse 11.

Ephraim is a reasonable guess, friend, but it isn't the tribe in the verse. The writer says "…our Lord descended from Judah, a tribe as to which Moses said nothing about priests." (Hebrews 7:14). So Jesus comes from a tribe Moses never spoke of for priests. That's why the writer goes on to say another priest like Melchizedek appears (Hebrews 7:15).

Right, baker! The writer says the law made nothing perfect, and then "…a better hope is introduced, by which we draw near to God." (Hebrews 7:19). Drawing near is what that better hope brings. After hearing the law made nothing perfect, that's good news.

Altars do come up in this passage, friend. But when the writer says what the better hope does, it's this: "…a better hope is introduced, by which we draw near to God." (Hebrews 7:19). Drawing near to God is the answer.

Yes, baker. "Because of this oath, Jesus has become the guarantee of a better covenant." (Hebrews 7:22). The oath and the guarantee go together. The oath is what God said to Him: "The Lord has sworn and will not change His mind: 'You are a priest forever.'" (Hebrews 7:21).

Yes, baker. "He sacrificed for sin once for all when He offered up Himself." (Hebrews 7:27). Notice ONCE FOR ALL. The other high priests offered daily sacrifices, first for their own sins and then for the people's, and Jesus doesn't need to do that.

Right, baker! "…the oath, which came after the law, appointed the Son, who has been made perfect forever." (Hebrews 7:28). The law appoints as high priests men who are weak, but the oath appointed the Son. That's quite a way to finish a chapter.

Prophet is a fair guess, friend, but the verse is about priests. The writer says "…the law appoints as high priests men who are weak; but the oath, which came after the law, appointed the Son, who has been made perfect forever." (Hebrews 7:28). The one the oath appointed is the Son, not a prophet.
